“Before the hold, and the hold is old.” He does not slow down. “There is no wind down here. There has never been a wind down here. It hums in one anyway, and Karn Dolur will tell you that is the span settling, and the span has been settling for nine hundred years.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A toll post on a road the guild stopped tolling, three dark lamps above it, and a man sitting under them with a book.
“No toll,” he says. “Has not been for two hundred years. I sit here.”

options.text: Three lamps out, all by you.
You are the only person who sits on this road. Does the bridge sound right to you?
The tally. Every year of it.

says.text: “All three, and I have sat under them for thirty years.” He does not look up. “They went out one after another, a year apart, and they went out in order going away from me.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“It sounds hollow at the ends.” He says it as a fact about masonry, which is how he has kept it bearable. “Ring what it stands on and it answers. Ring the cliff and it does not. There is a room in each pier and there has been the whole time.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He hands it over without looking at it. “Three years in a different ink,” he says. “Not my father's hand and not mine. I have never worked out whose, and I have had thirty years of sitting here to work it out in.”
“It is the post's,” he says. “I am the post.”
A crossing over the Sunless River, a lamp on a tripod, and a woman scribing onto brass with the river going past under her.
“Do not stand in the light. I am taking an angle off the far bank.”

options.text: The shaft above the Weeping Vault.
You measure things. What is the interval on the market road's lamps?
The plate. The one with the number scratched out.

says.text: She puts the scriber down. “It goes up further than there is rock above it.” She lets you have that. “I sectioned it. I took the depth from the surface and I took the height of the shaft and the second is bigger. I wrote the number down and then I scratched it out, because a number like that gets a surveyor retired.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Warm and salt.” She is precise. “There is no sea within four hundred miles of straight down from that hall. I have tasted it and I have had it tasted by somebody who did not know where it came from, and they said seawater.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Twice what you would light a road at, and exact between one and the next.” She does not have to check. “I took it as a young surveyor because it looked wrong. It is wrong, and it is *consistent*, which is worse. A lamp interval drifts. That does not.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

She fetches it and turns it so the scratched-out corner is toward you first, which is either honesty or relief. “Eight pillars on it,” she says. “Go and count them, and then come back and tell me I sectioned it wrong.”
“It is scribed for the guild,” she says, and does not look at the corner. “Ask me the measurements.”
Four hundred sheep on short turf over white rock, and a man in the middle of them working a pair of shears without looking at them.
“Mind the flock. Say what you want, I will hear you.”

options.text: You have walked over it all your life. What shape is it?
The rod you keep the count on. Lend it to me.

says.text: “Three parishes. Us, Thrift, and the Cobbleway lot who come out in carts and are no use.” He shears on. “Ask any of the three why and you will get the same answer, which is that the other two turn out and it would look bad not to. That is the whole of the reasoning and it has run four hundred years.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

Ansel stops, which he does not do. “It has corners on it,” he says, carefully, like a man who has never said it aloud. “You cannot see them from the road and you cannot see them from the green. You can see them from on it, and once you have you cannot stop.” He goes back to the sheep. “Nothing that runs has corners.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He fetches it out of the thatch, which is where it has always lived. “There are more notches on that than the parish has years of records,” he says. “I have never known what to do about that, so I have gone on cutting them.”
“It goes back in the thatch,” he says, and it does, and that is the end of the conversation.
A first-floor office over the mole with every window facing water, and a berth list going down a slate faster than it comes off.
“If it is a berth you want, it is tomorrow. If it is anything else, be quick.”

options.text: The tower on the head. Has anything been in it?
The way in under the head.
The night book. I want to read it.

says.text: “Four times.” She does not look up from the berth list. “1187, 1224, 1251, and eleven years ago, which I saw. Same week of the year every time.” Now she looks up. “There is no stair in that tower. There has never been a stair in that tower. I have had the masons out.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Bottom of a spring tide, and it shuts again inside the hour.” She taps a tide table she has clearly consulted for other reasons. “Which means anybody who has ever gone in has either come out very fast or has not come out. We have never recovered one.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

She puts it on the counter and keeps a hand on it. “Fourteen hands going back to before the mole was built,” she says. “Every one of them writes the same correction and not one of them says what for. If you find out, come back. I will have kept the page.”
“It is the office's,” she says, “and I am the office,” and puts it back under the counter.
She turns the berth list over and goes on writing on the back of it.
A front room with a table, a strongbox and a book, and a man who has been bailiff long enough that the room has stopped being a front room.
“Strays, fees, and the pinfold. Which is it?”

options.text: Why will the coach horses not stand there?

says.text: The bailiff does not pretend not to know what you mean, which is itself an answer. “One a year. Same night. Taken up, unclaimed, and the fee paid.” He closes the book. “My father wrote it. His father wrote it. I have written it nineteen times and I have never once been in that yard to see what I was writing about.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Because they are not stupid.” He says it flatly. “One night of the year they will not go through the gate and they will not be made to. The stablers stopped trying before I was born and put the night in the coaching timetable instead, which tells you how long this has been the arrangement.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He hands it across with both hands, which is not how a man hands over a ledger. “The October line is eleven words and it names where the beast was put,” he says. “I have read it nineteen times. I would rather somebody else went and looked.”
“It is the town's book and I am the town's bailiff,” he says, which is a sentence he has clearly had ready for years.
The last field before four hundred feet of nothing, and an old farmer leaning on a gate looking inland rather than out.
“I have looked at that hill for sixty years. Go on, then.”

options.text: You have looked at it for sixty years. What is it?
The birds on the head. Is there anywhere they don't nest?
Somebody pays the October fee at Cobbleway.

says.text: “It is not a horse.” Tibb says it without any weight at all, the way you say a thing you settled long ago. “From up the cliff path you can see two of the cuts go square to each other, and they run on past where the beast would stop.” A shrug. “I told the vicar once. He wrote it down and nothing happened, which is what I expected.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Round the tower's foot. Forty feet of bare rock, near enough a circle.” Tibb spits over the gate. “There is guano a foot deep on every other stone of that headland. Birds are not sentimental. If they will not sit there, there is a reason and it is not history.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“In coin, into the box, every year.” Tibb has clearly thought about this. “Now a fee is paid by the owner. So somebody owns it, and has for two hundred years, and has never once come and collected the animal they are paying for.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Eleven boats up the shingle above the tide line, and a woman going over the seams of the nearest one on her knees.
“If you are buying fish it is up the beach. If you are asking about the water, ask.”

options.text: Do you change course off the head at night?
The standing water on top of the downs.

says.text: “Two points to starboard.” Immediately, without thinking. Then she hears herself. “Everybody does. My father did. I have never asked him what for and he is dead now.” She sits back on her heels. “There is nothing there to clear. I have sounded it. There is nothing there.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Never dry.” She is definite. “Two summers ago the wells went at Thrift and the beasts were being walked four miles and that water was where it always is.” A grin with no humour in it. “On chalk. On the *top* of chalk. Somebody made that, and it was not this century.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Rope by the fathom, tar by the barrel, lamp oil, and a wall of charts with three of them turned face-in.
“Rope, tar, oil, glass. Charts if you promise not to sue me.”

“A way in, at the bottom of a spring tide.” He does not have to look it up. “Open about an hour. I have sold gear to four parties who meant to go in and I have had two of them back.” He straightens a coil. “I do not sell them the rope any more. They buy it at Gullmere and think I do not know.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Three sides are the town's and the fourth is not.” He is pleased to be asked. “I carted the lime up there when they repointed the good sides. Could not match the old face. Nobody can match the old face — it was mixed with something that is not in it any more, and it has not weathered in eight hundred years.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A stage house on a straight road, four horses out and four in, and a fare slate being rewritten faster than it can be read.
“Bed, bait, or the next coach. In that order of likelihood.”

options.text: How long is the Moot Road?
The oaks. Is there anything out by them?
The mile book. Let me take it.

says.text: “Eleven miles.” Pyle does not look up from the fare slate. “And fourteen marks on it.” A pause exactly long enough to be deliberate. “My great-grandmother opened this house and wrote fourteen in the book, and her son wrote fourteen, and I write fourteen. Nobody has ever bothered to be troubled by it but me.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“There is a lane.” Now Pyle looks up. “Six foot down into the ground, sides standing, no spoil either side of it. That is a hundred years of loaded carts.” The slate goes down. “Nothing has been down there in my life, my father's life, or the book.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

It comes off the shelf with a cloth round it, which tells you what the family thinks of it. “Every stage and every fare since the house opened,” Pyle says. “And every one of us counting to fourteen. Find out which three, and come and tell me, and I will stand you whatever you like.”
“It is the house's,” Pyle says, and the cloth goes back round it, and back on the shelf.
A covered burn the size of a cottage giving off no visible smoke at all, which took forty years to learn, and a woman watching it.
“Do not stand upwind and do not touch the sides.”

options.text: What is the line you will not cut inside?
The charter. I want to see the back of it.

says.text: “All of an age and none of them old.” Moll rakes over a section of the burn that does not need it. “A wood does not do that. Leave any gap in this wood and in four years it is thicket and in twenty it is wood again. That has been forty yards wide for longer than the Moot Road has existed.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

She walks you to it, which takes a quarter of an hour, and stops at a place with nothing at it. “Here.” Then along, a hundred paces, still nothing. “And here.” She turns round. “Every burner in Rooksrest can do that and not one of us can tell you what we are walking. We learned it off the last lot. They learned it off theirs.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

She unrolls it on a stump. The front is the parish's right to cut, in the parish's clerk's hand. The back is a line drawn freehand, closed, with no words on it at all. “That is not our writing,” Moll says. “That is not anybody's writing. That is a shape.”
“It is the right to feed forty people,” she says, rolling it up. “No.”
She walks round to the far side of the burn and stays there.
A hut with a swept step, a hearth in use, and somebody in the doorway who heard you coming a long way off.
“You are four days from a field. Say what brought you.”

options.text: The marks are further out than the survey.
The rod. Lend it to me.

says.text: “Not me.” Kest says it fast, which is the most interesting thing about the answer. “I keep the hut. I have kept it eleven years. I am not on the parish roll and I have never been paid a quarter in my life.” A long look out at the trees. “The faces get cut. I have sat up for it twice and both times I woke where I sat and it was done.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Eighty yards.” No hesitation at all. “I have chained it. Twice, in different years, and it was not the same eighty both times.” Kest looks at you properly for the first time. “It is going out. Slowly. And the field is where the field has always been, so nobody in Fenny Cross has noticed a thing.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

Kest takes it down off two pegs. “Sixteen and a half foot, and worn smooth at both ends,” Kest says. “I have had it eleven years. Somebody wore those ends and it was not me and it was not in eleven years.”
“It came with the hut,” Kest says. “It stays with the hut.”
A cart backed under an eave, one wheel off, and a man doing something to the hub he is clearly not enjoying.
“Coast road or forest road? I will complain about either.”

options.text: You've counted the marks on the Moot Road.

says.text: “Every trip.” Dunn wipes the hub. “Three of them are not on the road. They are off it — twenty yards, forty, sixty. I used to think they had shifted the road round them.” He straightens. “Then I stood at one and sighted the other two and they line up with each other, and the line they make goes across the road, not along it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Crosses nothing.” He laughs, but not much. “Stream went round two hundred years back — there is the old bed, dry as a road. Bridge is pointed, parapet is sound, and I have carted every load of lime that has gone into this parish for twenty years and not one of them went there.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Sacks by the hundredweight, a set of scales worn to a shine, and a man who has just told somebody their charcoal is damp.
“By the sack or by the load. Damp is half price and I will know.”

options.text: The mile oaks. Were they planted?

says.text: “Struck.” Ives is definite. “Every one of them off the same tree — you can see it in the leaf, they are all the same leaf, and oak is not shy about being different.” He weighs something. “I have looked for the mother tree for thirty years. It is not on the road and it is not off it either, and I have been most of the way to Elderhollow looking.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“The parish pays one.” He puts the weight down. “Quarterly. Four hundred years of quarters, in the parish book, never missed.” He shrugs. “Ask Fenny Cross who it is. Ask the vicar. Ask Kest, who lives in the hut and is not it. Nobody knows and the money goes.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A low taproom with everything in it damp, a fire that is winning, and a landlady who has already put a mat down for you.
“Boots by the fire. Both roads meet here, so I hear both.”

options.text: Does anything cross it at night?

says.text: “That is the question, is it not.” She says it like somebody who has heard it before and never had a good answer. “Nine miles, dead straight, forty yards across. The Moot Road took the parish eleven years and a great deal of arguing with the wood.” A cloth over the bar. “Nobody argued about the Greenway. It was there.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“No.” Flat, and she does not soften it. “The deer go up it and down it. They will cross the turnpike, the coast road and my yard, and they will not step over the Greenway after dark.” She looks at the fire. “I have had drovers in here who lost a night going round rather than over, and they were not men who lose nights.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A yard of hurdles and tallies and a man going down a column with his thumb, twice, and then a third time.
“I am counting. You can talk while I count.”

options.text: The line of trees. What is it for?
How many trees are in it?
Your count. All forty years of it.

says.text: “It is for breaking the wind.” Serel says it the way you say the thing everybody says. Then, because you have not gone away: “The wind is off the south-west. Has been since before the Lines. And the trees run south-west to north-east.” A hand, flat, drawing it in the air. “They run *with* it. Eleven miles of doing nothing at all.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

Serel goes quiet for long enough to be uncomfortable. “I have counted it forty years,” he says. “Going north I get one number. Coming back I get another. I have done it in a day, both ways, sober, with a boy counting beside me.” He shrugs, and it is not a casual shrug. “The boy gets different numbers too, and not my different numbers.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He brings out a roll of it, which is more than you expected and less tidy. “It does not settle,” he says. “Forty years of it not settling. I have never shown anybody because there is no way to say it that does not sound like a man who cannot count.”
“It is forty years of looking foolish,” Serel says, “and it is mine,” and puts it away.
Eight horses on a line, four of them cooling, and somebody going over a hoof without seeming to look at it.
“Remount, message, or neither. Neither is fine, but stand clear.”

options.text: Is the planting in the Lines' record?
How do you know when the flood comes?
The flood book. Let me have it.

says.text: “No.” Talith does not need to check, which is itself the answer. “We have every foaling for nine hundred years. Every crossing. Every rider who did not come in.” A hand on the book. “Eleven miles of trees is a season's work for four hundred people and there is not one line about it anywhere. We do not fail to write things down.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“The grass tells you.” Immediate, and then Talith hears it. “That is what we say. Three days out, everybody moves stock, and we are never wrong, and the week is the same week.” A pause. “I have asked eleven riders what the grass does. I have had eleven answers. None of them is a thing the grass does.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

It is oilcloth-wrapped and it is heavy. “Nine hundred years of the same week,” Talith says, “written by people who each thought they were the first to notice. If you go down that bank in the dry, that book tells you how long you have.”
“It rides with the relay,” Talith says. “It has always ridden with the relay.”
Talith mounts a cooled horse and takes it twice round the post without a word.
A stone trough, a rope, and somebody sitting where they can see both the water and the road to it.
“Drink what you need. Fill what you carry. Do not wash in it.”

options.text: What is the hole beside it?
Somebody paid for that timber. Do you have the paper?

says.text: “Not in the record.” Ondir does not look at you; the watching is the job. “Nine hundred years. Droughts that took the Lines down to half their stock and it ran the same.” A nod south. “Two miles that way nothing has run since before anybody was counting. It stops. Here does not.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Shored.” Flatly. “Timber, cut and set, holding a way down. I have been in the first forty feet and the carpentry is better than my house.” Now Ondir looks at you. “There is no timber on this steppe. There is no mine on this steppe. Somebody carted the wood here and paid for it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

Ondir takes it out of a box that has nothing else in it. “Signed, sealed, and dated in a year we have not used for six hundred,” he says. “It came with the post. Every watcher gets it. Not one of us has ever gone down on the strength of it.”
“It comes with the post,” Ondir says, “and I have the post,” and the box shuts.
A camp in the lee of a bank a quarter of a mile from the other bank, and a fire in a ring of stones that is not this year's ring.
“There is room. There has been room here for nine hundred years.”

options.text: This bed is very wide for the water that comes down it.
The water at the Last Water.

says.text: “Four weeks.” Bree pokes the fire. “Four weeks of water and a quarter mile of bed. I have seen the flood — it is a frightening thing and it does not fill a fifth of this.” A look up. “Something cut this. The river only borrows it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Warm, and iron.” Bree makes a face. “Every spring on this grass is cold and tastes of grass. That one you could bathe a child in without heating it, and it leaves a taste like a coin.” A shrug. “Ondir says it has always been so. That is not the same as knowing why.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Four hundred head strung out along a line of trees, and a herder walking the length of them because that is what the day is.
“Walk with me or stand still. Do not stand in the middle.”

options.text: The trees. Were they all set at once?
Why will the Lines not camp at the Last Water?

says.text: “Within a season.” Kosh does not break stride. “You can see it in the boles — same girth, same lean, same scar year in all of them. Eleven miles.” A glance across. “Four hundred people for a season. On this grass, in that year, there were not four hundred people.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Ask twelve and you will get twelve answers.” Kosh sounds genuinely amused. “Bad grass. Bad ground. A cousin who died there. The Glasslands too close.” The amusement goes. “Now ask why none of the twelve is the same, when we agree about everything else on this steppe down to which side of a hill.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Hay by the load, girth straps, salt, and a woman who has already worked out what you forgot to bring.
“Hay, salt, strap, or rope. It is always one of the four.”

options.text: The camp at the crossing. Why is it there?
What is showing in the open face?

says.text: “Because it has always been there.” Ana stacks something. “Nine hundred years of hearths, one on top of the last. And there is no crossing — it is dry eleven months, and the twelfth you would not put a horse in it.” She stops stacking. “Nobody has ever *needed* to camp at that spot. They camp there anyway.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Stone.” She says it like it is an inconvenience. “Forty foot down, courses of it, dressed, laid level, going both ways into the bank.” A hand out flat. “Not fallen. Not washed. Laid. My father took a block out and it is my doorstep, and you can see the chisel on it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A shelf of rock halfway up nine hundred steps, a bench, a brazier, and somebody sitting with a broom across her knees.
“Sit if you are climbing. Everybody sits.”

options.text: Who pays you to sweep the stair?
Four generations of counting. I want it.

says.text: “Nobody.” Bel says it without any bitterness, which is the unsettling part. “The hold pays the railmen, the lampmen and the gate. Not the sweeping.” A shrug. “My great-grandfather started coming up because it wanted doing. It has never wanted doing. It is clean when I get there, every day, and I sweep it anyway.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Nine hundred and one.” Instantly. Then, watching your face: “The lintel says nine hundred. It has said nine hundred for six hundred years and the hold does not make that kind of mistake.” Bel shoulders the broom. “Four of us have counted. We all get nine hundred and one. We have never worked out which one is the extra.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

It is a folded sheaf, tied. “Every day, the count and the state of it,” Bel says. “Four hands and the same two things written down over and over: nine hundred and one, and already clean.” A pause. “If you find the extra one, do not tell the hold before you tell me.”
“It is the family's,” Bel says, and the sheaf goes back inside her coat.
A cottage with one window facing the road and a lamp burning in it at an hour that does not need a lamp.
“Road is open. If you have come to ask, it is open.”

options.text: Has the bell ever rung on an open road?
The watch book. The eleven nights.

says.text: Orn looks at you for a while. “Eleven times,” he says. “I have the nights. My predecessor had four of them and I have seven.” He turns the book round without opening it. “Every one of those nights the watch was asleep. Including me. Twice.” Flat. “I do not sleep on watch.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Worn on the inside of the turn.” He mimes it, hands round nothing. “You pull a bell rope, you wear the outside — the face away from the wall, where your grip drags.” The hands drop. “That rope is worn on the other face. To wear it there you would have to be standing where the floor is.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He hands it over faster than you expected, and you realise he has been hoping somebody would ask. “Take it. Read it in daylight.” He does not quite manage a smile. “Eleven dates. See if they are anything. I have looked at them for nine years and they are not moons and they are not weather.”
“It is the gate's book,” Orn says, “and the gate is mine tonight,” and puts it under the lamp.
He turns the lamp down and goes on watching the road, and does not watch you.
Rope, poles and crampons laid out in an order somebody would fight you about, on ice, in shade.
“Going to the ice? Then we talk about your boots first.”

options.text: Warm or cold, what comes out of it?
The hold's survey of the shoulder. Lend it to me.

says.text: “Breathes.” Vesk says it like a fact about a road, which to Vesk it is. “In, then out, and you can keep the count on a watch. I have. Same count in a gale, same count in a dead calm.” A look up at the face. “Weather does not keep time. That keeps time.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Warm.” Vesk lets that sit. “North face. Shade from Emberfall to Greening. That rock has not thawed in any year anybody has written down, and there is warm air coming out of a hole in it, on a count.” A shrug that is not a shrug. “I take parties past it. I do not take them in.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

Vesk unrolls it on a rock and puts stones on the corners. Every hole, every fault, every fall of scree, to the inch — and then, where the mouth is, the ink simply stops and there is good clean vellum after it. “No note,” Vesk says. “The hold does not leave a margin. The hold has never once left a margin.”
“It is the guides',” Vesk says, rolling it. “Four of us alive can read it. Ask one of the other three.”
A wayhouse on a road with a hole in it, doing better trade than the road can account for, and a landlord who knows exactly why.
“Beds, stew, and I will tell you the road is impassable whether it is or not.”

options.text: The ice on the shoulder road.

says.text: “A room and a half, all of them, dug back into the slope.” Dorn wipes a table. “Except one. That one goes back seventy foot — I have paced it from the outside and the door is where the others' doors are.” He straightens. “In forty years nobody in that house has mentioned it and nobody next door has asked. That is not how villages work.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Will not form within forty foot of that mouth.” He says it cheerfully. “Which is why the guides take the parties that way and why they charge what they charge. Ask Vesk about it and see how fast the conversation is about boots again.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Rope, tallow, nails, boots, and a counter positioned so its keeper can see both the up road and the down.
“Going up or coming down? It changes what you need and what I charge.”

options.text: There are two stairs on that cliff.
Does anything nest on the broken stair?

says.text: “There are.” Hesk does not stop counting nails. “The one you climb and the one that came down in the rains. Go and stand on the broken one.” Now the counting stops. “The treads are short and deep. Ours are long and shallow, because we have legs. Whoever cut that one was working to a different leg.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“No.” He puts the nails down. “Gritstone face in this country, you cannot walk under an overhang without wearing it. Every ledge on that cliff is white with them.” A hand toward the window. “Not that flight. Not one nest, not one streak, the whole length of it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A forge dug into a slope, working, with the door open in weather that should have it shut.
“Mind the door stays open. I like it open.”

options.text: The hold has surveyed this mountain.

says.text: Ruvo does not answer for a while, and works. “It does,” he says eventually. “Goes down cold in the basket. Comes up you can feel it through the wicker.” The hammer goes down. “I said so once, in the Drift, in front of eleven people. Nobody argued and nobody looked at me and the subject changed. I have not said it since. You are the first.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“To the inch.” He is proud of it and then he is not. “Every hole, every seam, every fault, since the founding. I have seen the sheets — my father cut plate for the cases they keep them in.” A look toward the shoulder. “And the shoulder sheet stops at that mouth. Clean. No note. The hold *always* notes.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A cottage with a peat stack under the eave twice the size of the cottage, and a woman counting it who does not need to.
“It is my turn this fortnight. Talk while I carry.”

options.text: How long has the fire been going?
What happens on the nights it burns green?
The rota. Let me take it.

says.text: “Two hundred years and a bit.” Wenna says it the way you say your own age. “Colder kept it forty. The parish has kept it since, on the rota, and there is no gap in the rota — I have been through it twice looking for one.” A dry look. “Every parish record in Aurendel has a gap in it. Ours does not.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

The friendliness goes out of her, not unkindly. “Two nights a year. When the wind comes off the moor instead of the vale.” She looks at the door. “Everybody is inside by dark. Nobody rings a bell and nobody knocks and nobody has ever said out loud that we do it. I did it as a child before I knew I was doing it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

She hands it over in an oilcloth. “A hundred and sixty years of whose turn,” she says. “And two nights a year ruled straight through with nobody's name against them, every year, in every hand.” A beat. “Somebody keeps it those nights. It has never gone out.”
“It is the parish's and it is my turn,” Wenna says, and the oilcloth goes back in the dresser.
Duckboards out over black water to a face of cut turf twelve feet high, and a man on the top of it working down.
“Stay on the boards. I mean that kindly.”

options.text: The bodies out of the deep peat.
The cutters' book. I want the two lines.

says.text: “Forty-one.” Hald leans on the spade. “I have carried three myself.” He is quiet a moment. “The peat down there is eleven thousand year. Everybody knows that, it is why the Library pays. And one of the forty-one had an iron buckle on it.” He meets your eye. “Iron is four thousand. I am a turf cutter and even I can do that sum.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“To the black band and not past it.” Instant. Then he hears the next question coming and answers it. “No, nobody told me. I was eleven and I stopped at it, and my hands stopped at it before I did.” The spade goes back in. “Take any cutter out there at night with no lamp and they will put a hand on that band first go.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He gets it from under a dry sack. “Forty-one out, forty-one back,” he says. “And two of them written up as going back different to how they came out, in Bram's grandfather's ordinary hand, as though it were an ordinary thing to write.” He does not let go of it at once. “I would rather know.”
“It is the cut's book,” Hald says, “and the cut is all of ours,” and it goes back under the sack.
One room, one door, one window, eleven miles of heather, and somebody who has clearly been alone long enough to have views.
“There is tea. There is not much else.”

options.text: You keep the estate's old map.
You can see Colder's Fire from here.
The map. Lend it to me.

says.text: “No roof since my father's time.” Ferrin does not look up from the fire. “And eight worn places in the flags in front of it, even as fence posts.” Now the look up. “Worn through. Grit does not wear through in a century unless somebody is standing on it, and there has not been a shoot off that house since before the roof went.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“They did not want it and I did.” He unrolls a corner of it without being asked, which tells you how often he looks at it. “Drives, butts, beaters' lines, the whole moor.” A finger on one line. “That one does not stop at the scarp. It is drawn over and down, and it is the same ink as the rest, which means whoever drew it drew it on the same afternoon and thought nothing of it.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Every night of my life.” Ferrin does not think it worth remarking on until he does. “Twice a year it goes green. I can see it go from this door, eleven mile off, and the lamps in the village all come on inside the same quarter hour and then they all go out.” He sets the cup down. “Nobody rings anything. They just go in.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

He rolls it properly before he hands it over, which takes a while and is the whole of what he thinks about it. “Eight in the line,” Ferrin says. “Seven of them you can walk to. The eighth is drawn where there is no ground.”
“It is the only thing in here worth anything,” Ferrin says, “and I am not sentimental about much,” and rolls it up.
He puts the map in the box, sits on the box, and looks at the fire.
Peat by the load, tallow, rope, and a slate with the parish's account on it in a hand that has clearly added it up twice.
“Load, half load, or the parish's account. It is usually the parish's account.”

options.text: How much peat does the parish buy for that fire?

says.text: “Eleven loads a year.” Ivy taps the slate. “I have sold it eleven loads a year for nineteen years.” She puts the chalk down. “A fire that size, going day and night, eats thirty. I have said so to the vestry twice. Both times somebody said *well, it has never gone out, has it* and that was the end of the meeting.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Draw up.” She is definite. “Every hole on this moor breathes down — cold air falls, that is all it does. Put a candle at any of the ones under that edge and it lies flat the wrong way.” A shrug. “The shooting parties used to think it was funny. There have been no shooting parties for a while.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A taproom built to be found from a long way off, with the door on the moor side and a lamp in every window of that wall.
“Bed, fire, or the fire. Most people want the fire.”

options.text: Colder. What do the parish records say about him?
What do the cutters say comes out of the deep cut?

says.text: Sask leans on the bar with the air of a man who has been waiting years. “Buried twice,” he says. “Forty year apart. Same hand — the register was kept by one clerk for fifty years, so it *is* the same hand — and the same three words written after the name both times.” He straightens. “I have shown four people. Three said it was a copying error. The fourth was a Library man and he went very quiet.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“One day a year, in their thousands.” He says it without wonder, which is worse. “Out over the drop and down. My father counted them out and counted them back for eleven years because he did not believe the first ten.” A cloth on the bar. “Fewer come back. Every year. Never once the same number.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

“Forty-one, and I have heard about all forty-one in here twice.” Sask is enjoying himself, and then is not. “The one they will not let go is the buckle. Iron buckle, on a body out of eleven-thousand-year peat.” He turns a glass over. “The Library man said the face must have slumped. Hald carried that one up the boards himself and Hald says the face was clean.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
Turf stacked by the thousand under a long open shed, scales, and a book on a stand that has been in that spot a very long time.
“By the thousand or by the load. The book stays here.”

options.text: How many have come out of the deep cut?
Were the forty-one put back the ones that came out?

says.text: “Forty-one.” Bram does not have to check and does not pretend to. “Since we started counting, which is my great-grandfather.” He turns the stand slightly, not enough to show you the page. “And forty-one put back. That is in there too. The Library takes them, the Library measures them, the Library sends them home, and we put them back where they came from.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.

It takes him a long moment. “No,” he says. “Two of them are written up different going in to coming out. Different height on one. Different hands on the other — *hands*, written just like that.” He shuts the book. “My grandfather's hand, in among the weights and the dates, like it was a Tuesday.”
“I've said all I mean to,” they say, and go back to what they were doing.
A Keeper in a fungus market four miles under the world, with a board in front of her and one sheet pinned to it.
"You are the one who did the ninth," says Hesper. "Sit down. I have a list."

"Nine doors. Opened in order, over eleven hundred years, and everybody in my order has spent their career on the ninth because the ninth was open." She turns the sheet round. Eight lines. "These are the eight nobody watched. They were opened first. Whatever came out of them has had between four hundred and eleven hundred years to find somewhere quiet."

"Under the places you made safe." She does not soften it. "The ward cellars at Highpass. The undercroft at Barrowgate. A root cellar in the Hollow Beeches with a floor under the floor." A finger on the first three lines, each struck through in red. "Those three are already struck out. In red. I did not strike them out and neither did any Keeper living."

options.text: Then we start at the first one.

says.text: "Two conditions and they are not mine, they are the door's." Hesper counts them off. "Come at it properly levelled, because the thing behind it has had four hundred years and you have had one. And wear something out of the quiet half of this continent — a cloak, a hood, whatever you brought up out of a thread nobody set you on."
"The bar on that cellar door is on the inside. Think about what that means before you pull on it."
Hesper has the sheet off the board and flat on the table. Three lines struck through in her own hand now, over the red.

"Three," she says. "In one season. My order has managed nine in eleven hundred years and eight of those were the same door twice." She signs the bottom of it and pushes it across. "That is a warrant. There are five lines left on it and the next two are worse."

quests.name: The Open Door
quests.description: The Dene Barrow's door has stood open for six hundred years and never once mattered. Something about that has changed.

stages.name: Go and look
stages.description: Hedda says the draught has turned. Air used to go in.

objectives.description: Climb the sheep field to the barrow.

stages.name: Whatever came out
stages.description: It has been down to the village twice.

objectives.description: Put down what has come out of the mound.

stages.description: Hedda will know who that is.

objectives.description: Tell Hedda what is in the barrow.

objectives.description: Take the road east to Aurenhal.
Find somebody in the capital who will hear it.

quests.description: Vail will give you the run of the undercroft and a seal that opens gates, on the condition that none of this is discussed.

objectives.description: Take Vail's commission.
Read the Wardlist in the Kingshold.

quests.description: Orrin will not give you the Wardlist. He will leave you alone on the fourth floor for an hour, which he considers a different thing.

objectives.description: Hear what Orrin wants in exchange.
Get the Wardlist off the fourth floor.

stages.description: The stair is behind the storerooms and nobody sweeps it.

objectives.description: Go down into the undercroft.

objectives.description: Put down the Door-Warden.

objectives.description: Reach the Thornward.
Find somebody who tends it.

quests.name: The Thornward

stages.description: The way down is where the Wardlist says it is.

quests.description: Every ward on the list is a door in the same wall, and the wall has a corridor behind it.

objectives.description: Find a way into the Deeproads.

quests.name: Lantern Deep
quests.description: Nine hundred people in a cavern, and a lamp hanging over them on a chain nobody can account for.

objectives.description: Reach Lantern Deep.
Hear what the Wayfinders know about the Lantern.

quests.name: The Eleventh Chamber
quests.description: Ten chambers give a word back four times. The eleventh does not give it back at all, and the far door does not open until something is said correctly.

stages.name: The ten that answer
stages.description: You stop talking somewhere around the second.

objectives.description: Reach the Echo Halls.

stages.name: The one that does not
stages.description: Two keys, and the phrase cut over the tenth door.

objectives.description: Open the Echo Ward.

quests.name: Behind the Ninth Door
quests.description: Two hundred and eleven doors down the Long Hall, and nine of them stand open. This is the ninth.

stages.name: Down the Long Hall
stages.description: Four miles, dead straight, and the ceiling is not in your lamplight at any point.

objectives.description: Reach the ninth door.

stages.name: What has been on the other side
stages.description: It has been there as long as there has been a door.

objectives.description: Face the Keeper of the Ninth.

quests.name: The Unsealing
quests.description: The wards were shut by something, once. It is still hanging over Lantern Deep on a chain, unlit.

objectives.description: Light the Great Lantern and shut all nine.
Go through the ninth door and finish it from the other side.
Let Karn Dolur seal the Deeproads behind you.
Decide how this ends.

quests.name: Out of Season
quests.description: The eels stopped running past the drowned chapel in Harvest. Nesh has kept six huts standing through two months of weather to find out why.

stages.name: Go and look at the chapel
stages.description: It stands in the water at anything above summer level, and it is a long way above summer level.

objectives.description: Walk out to the Drowned Chapel.

stages.name: What is in the nave
stages.description: Something has been in the flooded nave long enough to have cleared the reach of everything else.

objectives.description: Deal with what is in the chapel.

stages.name: Tell Nesh
stages.description: She has been waiting two months to be told something.

objectives.description: Bring word back to the eel camp.

quests.name: What the Barge Was Carrying
quests.description: Nesh says the lampreys came up the reach, and things come up a reach from somewhere. There is a barge on its side in the Oxbow that went down loaded and was never got out.

objectives.description: Find the sunken barge in the Oxbow Meadows.
See what is still in the hold.
Ask Nesh what a barge was doing carrying that.

quests.name: The Badger Hole
quests.description: The barge was carrying stone out of the hedge country, and it was carrying it *away* from something. A terrier went into a hole under a hedge bank last spring and came out the far side of the field.

stages.name: Find the hole
stages.description: A longer set than a badger digs, and the spoil outside it is fresh.

objectives.description: Get into the Hedge Setts.

stages.name: The far end, where the walls are cut
stages.description: It is a badger hole for about eight feet.

objectives.description: Put down what has been digging.

quests.name: What Came Up the Weir
quests.description: It is dealt with, and now somebody has to be told — which is a different question from whether anybody wants to hear it.

objectives.description: Have the chapel closed the old way.
Have the chapel closed by warrant.
See the chapel closed.

quests.name: Unlicensed
quests.description: Three of the guild went down at Kettle Yard in Lastmonth. Dree wants to know who else is under her city, and she does not want to ask the Watch.

stages.name: Find the way down
stages.description: Behind a wine-shop that is not a wine-shop. You will not find it by being told where it is.

objectives.description: Get down the Cellar Stair.

stages.name: Whoever is down there
stages.description: They are not guild. Guild wear the hood.

objectives.description: Deal with the men in the cellars.

stages.name: Tell Dree
stages.description: She will want to know what they were carrying, not what they were carrying it in.

objectives.description: Report to the guild.

quests.name: The Old Gaol
quests.description: They were digging *towards* something, and the direction is the only evidence anybody needs: the west range of the gaol, which was emptied after the fire and bricked up in a hurry.

objectives.description: Get into the Old Gaol.
Find what the brickwork is hiding.
Ask Dree what was bricked up after the fire.

quests.name: What Was Bricked Up
quests.description: The register was left on the desk with a name still on it. The guild has been walking round that corner of the under for sixty years and telling itself it was the damp.

stages.name: Through the west range
stages.description: Sixty years of brick, and it comes down in an afternoon.

objectives.description: Get into the Warren Cellars.

stages.name: The man still on the book
stages.description: He was not left the keys. He was left with them.

objectives.description: Put down the Gaoler.
